props.title: What Makes a Family

sections.content: **What Makes a Family (2001)** (2001) sits at a crucial intersection of LGBTQ+ cinema and legal drama, arriving at a pivotal moment for gay rights representation in mainstream media. This Lifetime original film, starring Brooke Shields and Cherry Jones, tackled same-sex parental rights years before landmark cases like Obergefell v. Hodges. It follows directly in the footsteps of groundbreaking films like **The Children's Hour** (1961) and **Making Love** (1982), but shifts the focus from coming out narratives to the legal and social struggles of established LGBTQ+ families.

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a significant shift in LGBTQ+ family representation on screen. While **Philadelphia** (1993) had broken ground with its portrayal of gay relationships, films like **What Makes a Family** (2001) and **The Next Best Thing** (2000) moved beyond crisis narratives to explore the day-to-day realities of same-sex parenting. These films helped pave the way for more nuanced portrayals in works like **The Family Stone** (2005) and **The Hours** (2002).

The legal drama aspects of **What Makes a Family** (2001) connect it to a longer tradition of custody battle films, though with a groundbreaking twist. Where Kramer vs. Kramer (1979) explored straight divorce and custody fights, this film brought same-sex custody issues into mainstream consciousness, predating similar themes in later works like **Any Day Now** (2012) and **Freeheld** (2015). sections.content: The production quality and mainstream casting of **What Makes a Family** (2001) marked a crucial shift from earlier, lower-budget LGBTQ+ films. Brooke Shields' involvement helped normalize these narratives for broader audiences, similar to how **Boys Don't Cry** (1999) and **Monster** (2003) brought LGBTQ+ stories to mainstream attention through star power and accessible storytelling.
